text: track. And the most dangerous part is something called a margin call. When the value of the assets in your account
falls below the required safety threshold, the brokerage demands that you deposit more money. If you cannot do so in time
the firm has the right to sell your shares to recover its loan, regardless of whether the price is favorable or
terrible at that moment. Here's where things usually go wrong. During a market crash, tens of thousands of people can receive
margin calls at once. They all sell, which pushes prices down even further. As prices fall, more people receive margin calls
triggering yet another round of selling. Imagine a line of people standing on a staircase. All it takes is for one
person to fall, and many of the people behind them may tumble too. And that is essentially what happened in South
Korea this year. But the roots of this crash lie in the way an entire generation has come to view investing
and getting rich. South Korea currently has one of the highest household-debt ratios in the world. Over the past two decades
household debt has continued to grow and is now equivalent to almost the country's entire GDP. By the end of 2025
total household credit was approaching 2,000 trillion won—an enormous amount. What is particularly important is that a large share
of this debt is connected to housing. South Korea has a rather unusual rental system called jeonse. Instead of paying
rent every month, a tenant gives the landlord a very large lump-sum deposit. In many cases, that deposit can be worth
as much as half the value of the home. In return, the tenant can live there for several years without paying
monthly rent. It sounds reasonable, but there is a problem: the upfront payment is huge. To rent a place, you already
need a substantial amount of money. When interest rates were low, this arrangement could work quite well. Money was cheap. Landlords
could invest the deposits, while tenants did not have to make monthly rent payments. Everybody seemed happy. But when interest rates
rose, many landlords began struggling to return those deposits when leases expired. And the people who felt the pressure first were
often the tenants. If you're young, the situation is even harder. The employment rate among young people is considerably lower than
